lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Owned the pick-path layouts for the fast-moving zone and the labor reports the shift leads used.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; the findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.

- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations while also covering night-shift supervision, updating the safety training slides, coordinating holiday temp hiring and running the forklift certification schedule, which raised inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5%.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Reduced freight costs by 15% by consolidating supplier pickups into regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.
- Built the weekly supplier scorecard for 40 vendors, which buyers used to renegotiate delivery windows with the five least reliable.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Cut average order lead time through the warehouse from 10 days to 5 while holding daily throughput constant and doubling work-in-process to keep pickers busy.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Checked the planned routes against 4 weeks of real delivery logs; planned drive times came within 5% of the actual ones.
- Shared the model and a one-page summary with the grocer's dispatch team, who piloted the routes on two trucks for a month.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Built a seasonal forecast for 1,400 products across three warehouses that more than halved stockouts and cut inventory by nearly $2M.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: The Crestway and food-bank bullets claim nearly identical forecasting results in different settings.
items.because: They describe similar scope and results, which may make a reader question whether the same achievement is attributed twice.

items.says: Experience is not in newest-first order.
items.because: Lakeview appears above the more recent Crestway role, disrupting the chronology.

items.says: The unrelated florist role leads Experience.
items.because: It draws attention away from the more relevant operations experience.

items.says: Education appears before Experience despite several years of post-degree work.
items.because: It delays the work history that better establishes the candidate’s professional direction.

items.says: The delivery line gives volume but not the result of the deliveries.
items.because: Volume alone does not show whether arrangements arrived on time or what value the work produced.

items.says: The wedding-order and cooler tasks do not show their outcome.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether orders were ready when needed or how the cooler work helped the shop.

items.says: The line does not say what the layouts or reports improved.
items.because: The reader cannot tell why they mattered operationally.

items.says: “Owned” names responsibility rather than a specific action.
items.because: It leaves the actual work unclear and hard to distinguish from routine responsibility.

items.says: The time reduction comes after the study description instead of leading the line.
Unrelated duties interrupt the link between cycle counting and the accuracy gain.
items.because: A scanning reader may not know which work drove the increase, and the duties make the line read partly like a task list.

items.says: The inventory-accuracy result is buried at the end of the line.
items.because: The clear result and scale of contribution are harder to see.

items.says: The strongest Lakeview bullet does not open the entry.
items.because: Opening with the accuracy gain would put the entry’s strongest evidence first.

items.says: The reorder-point line describes a process but not what changed as a result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it improved availability, reduced excess inventory or otherwise helped the business.

items.says: The scorecard line does not state what changed after buyers renegotiated delivery windows.
items.because: The effect on supplier reliability or another measurable result remains unknown.

items.says: The buyer-use detail comes before the outcome.
items.because: It delays the result in a quick scan.

items.says: The lead-time, throughput and work-in-process figures are inconsistent.
items.because: Under Little’s law, doubling average work-in-process at constant throughput cannot halve lead time.

items.says: The throughput constraint and work-in-process tradeoff obscure the main outcome.
The pilot is described without its operational result.
items.because: Truck count and duration show scale, but not whether deliveries improved or planned savings held.

items.says: The opening is too broad to show what the analysis involved or what changed.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what analytical skill was used or whether leadership adopted the recommendations.

items.says: “Made recommendations” does not name a specific action.
items.because: The broad phrasing leaves the work and its operational value unclear.

items.says: The broad opening does not connect the entry’s two warehouse improvements.
items.because: The intake and forecasting work read as separate accomplishments rather than a clear account of the project.

items.says: The one-day intake-to-shelf improvement lacks a stated comparison basis.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it came from measured before-and-after times or an estimate.

items.says: Passive voice obscures who mapped the intake process.
items.because: It hides the candidate’s role.

items.says: The forecast is credited with reducing stockouts and inventory without showing the intervening actions.
items.because: A forecast can inform purchasing and allocation, but does not itself change orders or inventory.

items.says: The stockout and inventory reductions lack a baseline or comparison period.
items.because: The reader cannot judge their scale or timeframe, and the inventory figure depends on how and when it was valued.

items.says: The strongest food-bank bullet does not open the entry.
items.because: Its specific scope and claimed outcomes are more concrete than the broad opening.
